title: Stablecoins and Depegs (The Bank Run Simulator)
objectives: Tell fiat-backed, crypto-collateralized, and algorithmic stablecoins apart
Understand the reflexive death spiral that breaks an unbacked peg
Walk through the Terra/UST collapse and what it taught the market

steps.title: Not All Stablecoins Are Equal
steps.body:
A <Term id="stablecoin">stablecoin</Term> is a price that is supposed to sit still at $1.00. What actually holds it there depends entirely on what sits behind it, and the difference between designs is the whole ballgame.

Three designs dominate:

- **Fiat-backed (USDC, USDT).** Real dollars and short-term Treasuries sit in custodial reserves. The <Term id="peg">peg</Term> is defended by a literal, audited bank account.
- **Overcollateralized crypto (DAI, USDH).** No dollars. Users lock more than $1.00 of crypto <Term id="collateral">collateral</Term> for every $1.00 minted, and <Term id="liquidation">liquidation</Term> bots sell that backing if it weakens.
- **Algorithmic (UST).** Nothing hard backs it. The peg rests on code and a volatile sister token that is minted and burned to absorb supply and demand.

The same $1.00 label hides three very different risk profiles. A fiat-backed coin depegs if its custodian fails. An algorithmic coin can depeg the moment confidence does.

steps.title: The Reflexive Death Spiral
steps.body:
Picture a bank with no vault and no cash — only a printing press that churns out shares of its own stock. While people believe the stock is worth something, the bank can pay every withdrawal by printing more of it. The moment belief cracks, printing more just makes each share worth less, which sends even more people to the exit. That self-feeding loop is a reflexive death spiral.

How it tightens:

- Confidence slips and redemptions spike as holders rush to convert into something safer.
- To honour those redemptions the protocol mints enormous quantities of its sister token.
- That flood hyperinflates the sister token and crashes its price.
- Because the stablecoin's backing *is* that sister token, its backing falls further, so more holders panic.
- Everyone sprints for the exit before reserves hit zero. A digital bank run, self-accelerating until the <Term id="peg">peg</Term> is gone.

The cruel detail is that the escape hatch and the poison are the same mechanism. The mint-and-burn engine that holds the coin steady on calm days is what detonates it on panicked days — and once the crowd turns, no external shock is needed.

steps.title: Case Study: The $40 Billion Terra/UST Wipeout
steps.body:
For over a year UST looked like magic: it held $1.00 while paying roughly 20% yield through the Anchor protocol. That yield was the bait. An algorithmic peg with no hard <Term id="collateral">collateral</Term> was the trap.

The endgame played out over days, not months.

- Large holders pull liquidity from the main Curve pool, thinning the market where UST could be swapped for other stablecoins.
- A handful of big sellers dump UST, nudging it off its <Term id="peg">peg</Term> and below the arbitrage-safe range.
- The protocol fires its mint-and-burn mechanism, minting trillions of new LUNA to absorb the UST being sold.
- LUNA's price collapses under the fresh supply, so the backing evaporates. UST holders accelerate their exit and the loop compounds.
- Within roughly 72 hours, LUNA falls from about $80 to $0.0001 and UST breaks down to about $0.05.

Over $40 billion in value was destroyed in May 2022. The lesson spread across every chain: a <Term id="stablecoin">stablecoin</Term> whose <Term id="depeg">depeg</Term> defence depends on ongoing confidence in a floating token is fundamentally fragile, because redemption pressure arrives fastest exactly when you can least afford it.

questions.prompt: Which stablecoin design holds no hard collateral and instead relies on code plus a volatile sister token to defend its peg?
options: Fiat-backed, because the dollars sit safely in a bank account
Overcollateralized crypto, because it locks extra crypto in a vault
Algorithmic, because a mint-and-burn arbitrage loop replaces hard reserves
Hybrid, because a custodian guarantees every single redemption
questions.explainRight: Algorithmic coins carry no hard reserves at all. Their peg is maintained by minting and burning a sister token, which works only while arbitrageurs keep the faith — which is exactly why it is the most fragile design.
questions.explainWrong: Fiat-backed coins hold real dollars and Treasuries, and overcollateralized coins lock extra crypto per dollar minted. The design with no hard backing and a volatile sister token doing all the work is the algorithmic one.

questions.prompt: For a fiat-backed stablecoin such as USDC, what is the primary thing standing between it and a depeg?
options: A steep interest-rate kink that repels sellers
Real dollar reserves and short-term Treasuries held with a custodian
A sister governance token that absorbs selling pressure
An on-chain oracle that resets the price every block
questions.explainRight: The defence is boring but strong: real dollars and short-term Treasuries held by a custodian. The peg is only threatened if that custodian fails or the reserves turn out not to match the supply.
questions.explainWrong: Interest-rate kinks belong to lending markets, sister tokens to algorithmic designs, and oracles report prices rather than back them. A fiat-backed coin depegs mainly when its custodian — not its code — breaks.

questions.prompt: A crypto-collateralized stablecoin requires you to lock $1.50 of ETH to mint $1.00 of the coin. What does this overcollateralization actually buy you?
options: A guaranteed 50% yield for the protocol and its founders
A buffer so that a fall in the collateral's price still leaves the coin fully backed
Complete immunity from market risk, since collateral can never fall below the debt
The ability to mint unlimited coins without posting any collateral
questions.explainRight: The extra $0.50 is a safety margin. If ETH drops, the collateral can fall meaningfully before it is worth less than the $1.00 of debt issued against it, which gives <Term id="liquidation">liquidation</Term> bots room to sell and recover the full value.
questions.explainWrong: Overcollateralization is not a yield and not magic immunity — it is a cushion. The extra collateral absorbs price drops before the system becomes underbacked, which is why <Term id="ltv">LTV</Term> limits exist. ETH can still fall; there is simply room to liquidate and still make depositors whole.

questions.prompt: During UST's collapse, the protocol minted trillions of new LUNA tokens. What did that actually do to the value backing UST?
options: It tripled LUNA's value and restored the peg
It had no effect, because LUNA and UST are unrelated assets
It froze all UST transfers until prices recovered
It crushed LUNA's price, so the token backing UST became nearly worthless
questions.explainRight: UST's backing was the ability to redeem into freshly minted LUNA. Printing trillions flooded the market and collapsed LUNA's price, so the asset meant to absorb demand was now worth almost nothing. The rescue mechanism accelerated the <Term id="depeg">depeg</Term>.
questions.explainWrong: Mint-and-burn does not create value from thin air. Dumping trillions of new LUNA pushed its price toward zero and removed the backing UST needed. The two tokens are tightly coupled by design, and transfers were never frozen.

questions.prompt: Why are overcollateralized stablecoins like DAI far more resistant to depegging than algorithmic ones?
options: Every $1.00 in circulation is backed by more than $1.00 of verifiable on-chain assets that can be liquidated
A government agency insures their full value against loss
They cannot be transferred without permission, so runs are impossible
They refuse to use liquidity pools, which removes all price pressure
questions.explainRight: The reserves exceed the outstanding debt, so <Term id="liquidation">liquidation</Term> can always recover more than enough to honour redemptions. The value is real and on-chain, not a promise resting on sentiment.
questions.explainWrong: There is no government insurance, and these coins trade freely in pools like any other. Their strength is that more than $1.00 of real <Term id="collateral">collateral</Term> stands behind every $1.00 issued.

questions.prompt: A coin is marketed as "algorithmic but partially crypto-collateralized." Why might partial collateral make a death spiral slower but not impossible?
options: Because partial collateral is purely psychological and changes nothing in a crisis
Because the collateral automatically grows as the coin drops, so the peg always heals
Because a reserve factor routes the collateral straight to the protocol's founders
Because hard collateral absorbs the first wave of redemptions, but once it is exhausted the reflexive mint-and-burn loop is the only defense left
questions.explainRight: Real collateral genuinely helps — it buys time and can cover modest redemptions. But if selling pressure exceeds it, the protocol falls back on the same reflexive loop that failed for UST. Partial backing moves the cliff further out; it does not remove it.
questions.explainWrong: Partial collateral is far more than psychological — it absorbs early redemptions and slows the run. But nothing makes collateral grow when prices fall. The weakness is that once hard collateral runs out, a purely reflexive loop becomes the last line of defence, and that loop has no floor.

questions.prompt: Two stablecoins both trade at $0.99. Coin A is fiat-backed with audited T-bill reserves; Coin B is algorithmic with no hard backing. What is the most accurate read?
options: Coin A's dip is likely a shallow arbitrage gap that reserves and redeemability tend to close, while Coin B's dip risks the reflexive spiral that has no floor
Both dips are equally dangerous, because a peg is a peg
Coin B is safer, because algorithmic code cannot be mismanaged by a custodian
Coin A is riskier, because bank reserves can be frozen by regulators, so Coin B is preferable
questions.explainRight: A one-cent dip in a fiat-backed coin is usually an arbitrage opportunity — buy at $0.99 and redeem or swap back toward $1.00, anchored by real reserves. In an algorithmic coin the same dip can trigger minting, dilution of the sister token, and a slide with no hard floor beneath it. Same price, different floor.
questions.explainWrong: A peg is not a peg — the mechanism behind it is everything. Fiat-backed dips are typically shallow gaps that redeemability closes. An algorithmic dip can ignite the mint-and-burn spiral that destroyed UST, because there is no hard asset to catch the fall.
